IV10-01.note: Wary is holding back from suspected risk; guarded is the only option about risk. hopeful reverses the expectation, curious reverses the distance, polite swaps risk for manners. All four are attitude words in one register, so nothing stands out, but none is a near-synonym either - fine for an easy opener.

IV10-02.note: Deft is about how well the hand does it. willing/patient/humble are all approach-and-character words; humble is the one with a real pull, for a student who half-hears deft as deferential.

IV10-03.note: Sluggish is the match on the heaviness axis; anxious is the opposite arousal state. forgetful is a quietly good trap - Lethe/lethargic share a root, and a student who reaches for the etymology lands on memory. I would call this easy rather than medium for Upper Level; lethargic is common-usage vocabulary.

IV10-04.note: Rudimentary = only the first principles. costly/formal/recent each report a different attribute (price, manner, age) and a rudimentary thing can be any of them, which is what makes them clean wrongs rather than tempting ones. recent is the one with traction, via rudimentary-as-undeveloped-therefore-new.

IV10-05.note: Goad = prod into acting. escort is the best distractor in the synonym half: a goad literally drives cattle along, so the driving/leading sense is genuinely reachable, and escort is where a student who has the image but not the meaning ends up. praise and imitate are clean wrongs.

IV10-06.note: Key is right and unambiguous. But the standard trap for INSOLENT is INDOLENT, and no option serves it - weary is tiredness, not laziness, so it does not catch the confusion it looks like it was aimed at. evasive and anxious are wrong for clear reasons no student would fight. The weakest distractor set in the batch; an idle or lazy option would have made this item earn its medium label.

IV10-07.note: Quandary = stuck between two courses; dilemma is exact. rumor/bargain/delay all name situations, which is the axis the explanation correctly identifies, but none is a live confusion with quandary. I would call this medium, not hard - dilemma is a word students at this level own, so the item is solvable from the key side even without quandary.

IV10-08.note: Resilient = springs back. slow to anger is the real pull: resilient people get described as even-tempered, so a student reasoning from connotation rather than definition can land there. Phrase options are parallel in shape and length, so no formatting tell.

IV10-09.note: Rife = everywhere at once. harmless/costly/brief each report a different property (damage, expense, duration) and a rife thing can be any of them - the same clean-wrong construction as 04. brief is the mild trap, presumably via ripe/rife slippage. Correctly labelled hard.

IV10-10.note: Penury = want of money. The distractor set is built on one parallel - solitude, exhaustion, confusion are want of company, strength, clarity - which is elegant and makes the item decidable for a student who knows the pen-/pecuniary root. A student who does not know the word gets no pull from any of the three, so these read more as clean wrongs than as traps.

IV10-11.note: Churlish = ungracious and sour toward people; surly is the match on that axis. idle is a reasonable trap through churl-as-peasant, timid and boastful are clean wrongs. Both key and best distractor are hard words, which makes the item genuinely hard rather than hard-looking.

IV10-12.note: Best synonym item in the batch. approve is a real trap out of bureaucratic usage - expedite my request gets read as approve my request - and postpone is the direct reversal, which catches anyone working from the pace axis but with the sign flipped. Two distractors wrong for two different reasons a student actually commits.

IV10-13.note: Arbiter = the one whose ruling settles it. sponsor/rival/witness are all roles present in a dispute, so the item tests which role decides, not whether you recognise the scene - the right design. witness is the live one. Labelled hard; I would say medium, since judge is reachable from arbitrate.

IV10-14.note: Palpable = obvious enough to be all but touched. The three distractors are each about a different dimension (frequency, age, timing) and none engages the touch metaphor, so they are clean rather than tempting; palatable, the obvious confusion, is not represented. Options are all two-word phrases, no length tell.

IV10-15.note: Hard rain plus completely gives soaked, and the collocation confirms it. tangled is a strong distractor: wet dog fur really does mat, so the student has to notice the sentence supplies rain and nothing about matting. Not enough to defend as a second answer - nothing in the stem is about texture - but it does the work a distractor should.

IV10-16.note: Missed watering plus days away gives wilted. Flagging the near-miss rather than voting it down: the stem puts the ferns on a WINDOWSILL, which supplies exactly the direct sun that scorched needs, and the explanation dismisses scorched by saying it would need direct sun - answering a version of the stem where the ferns are not in a window. The causal chain the sentence actually builds is no-water, and scorched means burnt rather than dry, so wilted still wins on merit. But the explanation is arguing past the strongest objection, and moving the ferns off the windowsill, or having the explanation concede the sun and beat it, would close the gap.

IV10-17.note: The colon list is grip, position, pass timing, and every player is new - fundamentals. strategy is a strong distractor because two of the three listed items (where to stand, when to pass) genuinely read as strategy; only how to hold the stick rules it out, which is the right amount of work for an easy item.

IV10-18.note: The rule is entirely about duration - a different family each spring, never twice running - so permanent is what it prevents. Construction note: costly and profitable fail for the identical reason (the rule never raises money), so the four options are really three distinct wrongs, and the explanation says so itself in one clause covering both. One of the money pair could be spent on a duration-adjacent wrong (say hereditary or customary) that would actually contest the key.

IV10-19.note: Unchanged since the route moved = belongs to an earlier arrangement. provisional is a strong distractor for a student with the bigger vocabulary, which is the good kind of trap - it punishes reaching for the harder word instead of the accurate one - and unofficial is reachable for anyone who reads wrong as not authoritative rather than not current.

IV10-20.note: Stopped listening before answering, still accurate = produced automatically. impatient is the strongest single distractor in the sentence-completion half: the setup (same four questions all day, no longer listening) is exactly how irritation gets described, and the student has to notice the sentence reports no feeling at all. Explanation handles it correctly.

IV10-21.note: Same wedge on six visits = regular practice, and not an accident but a fixes the contrast. Same structural note as 18: misunderstanding and coincidence are one distractor twice over, both excluded by the same three words. They do catch a careless reader who skips not an accident, which is a real failure mode, so this is plausible rather than weak - but precaution is the only one that requires thought.

IV10-22.note: narrow but sets up the contrast, and the eight-hour round trip is evidence of depth rather than breadth. local is the working distractor - it picks up narrow and is refuted only by the drive. fragile and recent are clean wrongs. Correctly medium.

IV10-23.note: Although forces blank one against choked with snow, and an impassable route gets given up. The distractors are weak for a hard item: only one pair even survives the Although, so the second blank is never load-bearing and a student who tests the contrast alone is done. familiar . . . describe also echoes described from the stem, which is a small surface tell. Two-blank items are in scope for Upper Level, so the form is fine - it is the pairs that are underpowered.

IV10-24.note: The best-built item in the batch. Every option is an antonym pair, so the yet contrast discriminates nothing and the student is forced onto the colon: any-order chapters = a break with form, plain declarative sentences = the ordinary choice. That is a distractor set designed so the structural shortcut fails, which is exactly what this family needs.

IV10-25.note: New totals higher, weather unchanged, therefore the old gauge read low. rounded is a strong distractor - it is the other way a long-running figure goes wrong - and the explanation beats it on the right ground (rounding errs both directions). Small logical softness worth noting: moving the gauge two miles east could mean the new site is simply wetter, which would make the old figures accurate for the old site rather than understated. The stem blocks the easy version of that objection with not because the weather had changed, and the item reads county-wide, so the intended chain holds; it is a seam, not a defect.

IV10-26.note: The closest call in the batch and I am still voting exclusive. habitual is defensible-sounding: across the whole hour invites the reading that the modesty is a reflex rather than a response. What refuses it is the first clause - a story in which the failure turns out to be a virtue is a constructed move, and habit does not explain the reframing, only its repetition. on reflection also signals a revised verdict about motive, and entirely calculated is the idiom while entirely habitual is not. Strong distractor set: sincere is the first impression the sentence overturns, habitual the second-best reading, uncomfortable the wrong-axis one.

IV10-27.note: Trial plots in a warmer state promise more than a northern garden delivers, so the number reads optimistic. Labelled medium; I would call it hard - the vocabulary is easy but flattering is being used figuratively of a number, and the student has to carry warmer-therefore-faster through to the-figure-is-too-good. cautious is a strong distractor because it is the right axis with the sign reversed.

IV10-28.note: Set against though every one of them knew it the moment they heard it: the one thing they could not do is put it into words. perform is the distractor that does work, and the explanation kills it correctly on in words. recall and doubt are both refused by the same trailing clause, so again two distractors share one failure mode.

IV10-29.note: Friday four o'clock in August, no summary, no questions - every detail is a choice to satisfy disclosure while ensuring nobody looks. misquoted and contested are strong because both are what a committee normally fears, so the student has to see that this release is engineered against engagement of any kind, not against hostile engagement. celebrated is the clean wrong.

IV10-30.note: EXCLUSIVE FALSE - luck is defensible, and the stem's own wording is what defends it. Read it as written: its owner puts this down entirely to LUCK, since the shop happens to sit on the one corner where three bus lines meet. happens to is a chance marker, and the since-clause then reads as the justification for calling it luck - the shop did not choose or earn that corner, it fell into it. Paired with has never once advertised (success the owner did nothing to cause), luck is the modest attribution the sentence is set up for, and a modest owner crediting luck is the more natural story than one crediting location. The explanation does not engage this at all: it dismisses luck as mere chance and says the sentence points at a specific piece of ground - but pointing at the ground is equally the evidence for luck, since the stem frames the ground as an accident. Two clean repairs, either sufficient: delete happens to (the shop sits on the one corner), or replace the luck option with something on the location axis that fails (say foot traffic, which the corner would also support, or convenience). As it stands two options are defensible and the item should not ship.
